en: You raised a mighty calamity
And showed your own kin a stronger arm
Than ever you showed the enemy.
You felled the plane tree,
And brought down the towering mountain.
You left sixty young women and widows
Wailing without exception.
You displayed your senseless valor
And dressed the whole people in black.
Can a human being be like you?
You black-hearted madman—
Can such a one be called human?
Before the camel crossed the cliff,
My son, you gathered the Argyn to plunder.
You had your white-haired mother
Beaten by the Argyn.
You made my blood flow freely
And set my soul aflame.
When your mother had grown old,
You accustomed her to endless torment.
My mad son, sprung from my own eyes,
Was I to blame for some ancient blood-feud,
That you had me dragged by a blue-gray calf?
You roused my long-buried fury;
Old Bakai, venerable as your forefather,
Without killing or disposing of him,
You had dragged about like a wolf-game carcass.
When your mother wailed aloud,
You had her breast split open.
You inflicted utter humiliation;
An enemy would be far better than you.
You made the torment surpass all bounds,
And made sorrow flourish in my heart.
You had me dragged by a blue calf
And branded my breast.
You did it not once but a thousand times,
And made such strife that you surpassed
Every other son born of humankind.
You drenched my poor head in blood
And sheared my hair like a mare’s.
In my old age you punished me
And reduced my food to scraps.
You left me no more than a spoonful of blood
And scorched my soul.
You ruined and scattered my herds;
You bent my waist fivefold.
Bringing calamity upon this head,
You deeply wounded my heart.
Though I begged, you did not heed my words;
You darkened all my days,
And stirred up, my foal, every last trace
Of my far-distant fury!
You created the most terrible strife,
Let it become a deed never forgotten.
Let his world collapse and be leveled;
Let his affairs burn and be set right.
For the many souls who will remain behind,
Let the destroyer of nations perish,
And let the people’s affairs prosper!”
Your beloved mother Kanykey,
Her wrath full against Kanchoro,
Spoke openly of the enemy,
Every word taking a different turn.
If you attend to every word,
Each word of your wise, fierce mother,
If you consider every word,
Was like a thrust of a spear.
Külchoro, son of Külüstan—
Against Külchoro himself
Her aspect was stern, her venom strong,
Able to humble anyone who opposed her;
So Kanykey stood urging them on.
Her grief and anguish broke open,
The turmoil within her burst forth,
Her eyes opened wide as bowls.
Without another word or sound,
Your dear mother fell silent,
And Kanykey abandoned her speech.
Then the noble-born Aichürök—
I, the wretched one, began to speak.
Taken as booty by the enemy,
Her heart scorched because of the foe,
The grief-stricken unfortunate woman
Cast forth her heavy sorrow.
Before the wrathful khan,
Aichürök began to speak:
“Without seeing Judgment Day
Or hell, you have returned, dear brother-in-law;
After spending many years in slavery,
Letting much of your life pass,
And enduring many torments,
From the true world whence none return,
You have returned without going there, dear brother-in-law.
Before all the people can safely depart,
Curse all that you have done!
The camel has fallen from the cliff;
Your deeds are finished, my son!
You brought it to ripeness before it was ripe;
Kanchoro, who deserved to burn when ripe,
You burned before his time.
He burned and blazed into embers;
His head was severed and blood flowed,
And my son vanished from this world.
Heap upon him the hell within your grasp;
Inflict humiliation upon him like a sheep.
Until my children begin to move,
Rip his belly open like a melon.
Cut off his head like a sheep’s;
From the enemy who inflicted this torment,
Turn away only when your eyes close.
Bind both his hands,
Gouge out both his eyes,
Stretch him out and beat him like a hide.
Return his own devilry to him,
Without spilling or omitting any of it!
Pierce his neck while he still lives;
Take a blunt knife that cannot cut felt,
And cut him with that knife.
Flay his skin while he is alive;
Kill him amid torment,
And for seven days keep the wretch wailing—
Neither killing nor releasing him,
Nor bringing his punishment to an end.
Spread the rack wide,
Grieve him and torture his soul fiercely,
And take your vengeance fully.
Ravage the wretch
And stretch him over the bare rock.
Return all his own deeds to him
Without spilling or omitting any.
If his soul is strong enough not to die,
Let the wrathful swine remain alive.
For a mortal bound for Judgment Day—
You have kindled a smokeless fire.
You began with fierce wrath,
You cast your head into calamity.
You cooked him before he was ripe,
Kanchoro, destined to die when ripe,
You burned him before he could burn,
You warrior who will burn to death!
You bloodied the mouth of my gate,
You trampled Talas into dust,
You seized Ala-Too for your land,
You oppressed the Kyrgyz and made them your subjects.
Poor women and young children,
Bent old folk and growing youth—
Why did you abase them so?
Having deprived me of my hero,
Is courage and valor yours?
Was he one to be given as spoil to the enemy?
Was your protector’s vengeance ours to bear?
Yesterday, smashing and toppling the house,
Felling and bringing down the plane tree,
The inheritance left by our fathers,
The far-sighted one who saw from afar,
Before whom the earth split and shook,
My lion father who passed into the other world,
The one befriended by my lion father,
Who sharpened steel and shared his heart,
Who spoke with the smith David,
He was the keeper of the treasury,
The guardian giant of the khan’s wealth.
No man could ever encounter his like;
Among all sons of humankind,
Even Baabedin could not find one like him.
The master smith Bölökbay,
An eagle on the narrow cliff,
The inheritance left by our fathers—
You made him demand the treasury,
Driving him clamorous like a lean sheep,
With forty Kalmyks, Bölökbay
You contrived to settle his account.
Shouting as you handed him a sword,
The countless riches left by the hero,
As booty among the Jediger—
I did not come to take them, dear brother-in-law.
Where is your magnanimity, where is the lion?
Where is the strength on which we relied?
Born superior to mortal men,
Who struck terror into the enemy,
When sent in front, a bringer of fortune,
From behind, a vast army with ridged ranks.
Where are our blessings, where is our strength,
Where are the people who gave us hope?
Having destroyed your bloodthirsty lord,
You have taken the palace and become khan,
Both reins and the single bridle
You have now taken into your hands.
You no longer look as you once did;
You have become a sultan!
Yesterday, when the gray-maned wolf died,
When all the world was made into plunder
And apportioned by the measure of a whip,
You loaded mourning goods on the pacer,
You abandoned the palace to pillage.
You had trench upon trench dug,
The great palace left by the khan
You led away amid cheers and much urging,
And drove it into Jediger hands.
Making me render my account,
Making wounds split across my breast,
You utterly exhausted my tears,
You made my head a prize.
You let the loathsome enemy drink
The funeral feast left by the gray-maned wolf.
You disgraced all my hopes and desires;
Alas, there is a God to judge your cruelty.
You made them call him another man’s son,
My child left of my khan.
Every day you seared my soul;
By giving me as booty to the enemy,
You burned my soul again and again.
You became my enemy and cast me aside,
But God has freed my hands!
I have come to dig your grave,
I have come to cut off your road!
Now I will bind your fortune,
I will tear your throne away!
I will tear down your roof-ring and level it,
I will turn spring into autumn before its time.
My fury has come; I will lay you flat,
I will hack your life away in pieces,
I will swallow your blood like kumis.
I will end your reign as khan,
I will crush and chew your liver.
You burned me before I could burn;
May you burn and become an ember like me,
Blazing and consumed by fire,
May you vanish as I nearly did.
May you see no daylight, but only night,
May you become charcoal, may you become ash.
You wronged me not once but a thousand times;
Swaggering and strutting,
Why did you stir up so much strife?
From the very beginning, warrior,
Ninety beasts were slaughtered for your feast,
And from the first, mighty Kanchoro,
You were given the name Kanchoro.
You became a brother born of one nest,
But at heart you became an enemy.
You ruined the country and destroyed the people,
You spilled blood and slaughtered the khan.
You plunged the old into misery,
You brought evil upon everyone.
As though the Kyrgyz and Argyn did not exist,
You drove them all away together,
Disdaining them, you put out their hearths.
You increased your levies;
Why did you make them suffer so?
You drowned your fold in blood,
You carried your cruelty beyond all bounds,
You concealed your true malice,
You spread your conflict throughout the land.
Stirring bitter turmoil and strife,
You let the Jediger raid us.
